/technology/2026/nov/12/nvidia-ceo-jense.headline: A timeline of the affair scandal that sank Nvidia’s Jensen Huang
/technology/2026/nov/12/nvidia-ceo-jense.excerpt: Jensen Huang has stepped down as CEO of Nvidia, the company at the center of the AI boom, after leading it for more than 30 years. Huang, an electrical engineer by education, stewarded the company from a $1bn firm when it went public in 1999 to a company valued at more than $4tn in 2026. But in a matter of days, after it was revealed he had an extramarital affair with a woman that US officials believe to be a Chinese spy, Huang managed to wipe more than $600bn from the company’s valuation. China has denied the accusations that it had tapped Alice Huang, the woman in question and a top executive at a datacenter company called Megaspeed, to be an intelligence asset, and called them a “smear”. US officials had reportedly started to monitor the Megaspeed executive after suspecting the firm was diverting powerful Nvidia AI chips to Chinese firms, in potential violation of export restrictions. The Biden and Trump administrations had prohibited US companies from exporting some of the more powerful AI chips to China over national security concerns. Just a week ago it seemed that Huang’s ouster was unlikely, but in the days since he first disclosed an affair and affirmed his commitment to the company, the New York Times reported that there was a second affair – this time with another Nvidia executive. A lot has happened in the last few days, but how did we get here? Here’s a timeline of what we know about Huang’s entanglements.
/technology/2026/nov/12/nvidia-ceo-jense.trail: CEO behind the meteoric rise of Nvidia stepped down after it was revealed he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy

/technology/2026/nov/12/nvidia-ceo-jense.headline: Who is Colette Kress, interim Nvidia CEO after Jensen Huang exit?
/technology/2026/nov/12/nvidia-ceo-jense.excerpt: The hunt is on for a new Nvidia CEO. It comes after a whirlwind week, which saw the company head and co-founder, Jensen Huang, resign amid multiple allegations of extramarital affairs, including one that involved an alleged Chinese spy and two with company employees. Nvidia immediately named Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, as the interim CEO. It’s possible she could stay on permanently, but the company could also name another candidate for the full-time role. Names that have been floated include Ian Buck, who manages Nvidia’s AI hardware and software products, and Rene Haas, a former Nvidia employee and the current CEO of Arm Holdings, a UK-based chipmaker. Whoever takes over from Huang will have tremendous sway in the burgeoning world of artificial intelligence. The entire AI ecosphere relies on Nvidia, which engineers advanced chips used to train AI models and power companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. Nvidia is also a central driver of the US economy and one of the world’s most valuable companies, with a market cap of around $4tn. Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993, is known as an ambitious and visionary CEO who had a hand in most all aspects of the business. He led in an unusual management style, having about 60 direct reports, giving him more control over the company’s daily functions.
/technology/2026/nov/12/nvidia-ceo-jense.trail: Chief financial officer, reportedly disparaged by Huang during summer meeting, to take over on short-term basis

/technology/2026/nov/12/nvidia-ceo-jense.headline: Jensen Huang built an AI kingdom. Now he’s gone, will Nvidia’s ramparts be breached?
/technology/2026/nov/12/nvidia-ceo-jense.excerpt: Can the AI economy survive without its “central bank”? What does Jensen Huang’s fall mean for the world’s second-most valuable company, and what might a tremor in its fortunes mean for the world? Nvidia’s sky-high valuation is based on the fact that it designs and sells the advanced AI chips, called graphics processing units (GPUs), that underpin the AI economy. Without these, AI models such as ChatGPT and Claude could not be trained and would not run. This has made the chipmaker arguably the most important player in AI and, at times, the most valuable company in the world. Huang’s departure sent shares in Nvidia plunging 13% in early trading. Nvidia is not the only company that designs these chips. Most leading tech companies, including Microsoft, Meta and Google, are trying to make their own lines of AI chips. Some of these, such as Google’s tensor processing units, appear to be at least as good as Nvidia’s, and even better for certain purposes. What makes Nvidia irreplaceable – and far more integral to the AI economy – is its web of relationships, most of these led by Huang himself. One aspect of this is Nvidia’s complex web of ties with the companies actually building AI infrastructure, a mess of circular finance that implicates US tech giants and many of the world’s governments. In recent years, Huang has been the kingmaker when it comes to AI.

/technology/2026/nov/12/nvidia-ceo-jense.headline: Thursday briefing: What we do (and don’t) know about Alice Huang and the Nvidia affair
/technology/2026/nov/12/nvidia-ceo-jense.excerpt: Good morning. Espionage is supposed to be a secretive business, and spies are supposed to be virtually invisible. That hasn’t been the case for Alice Huang, the mysterious Shanghai executive who formed a romantic relationship with Jensen Huang, the founder of Nvidia, one of America’s most powerful tech companies. Many questions have arisen since it emerged that US intelligence believes that Huang (no relation of Jensen’s) is an asset recruited by the Chinese intelligence services to spy on behalf of Beijing. This morning’s newsletter explains what we know about the story, and what it tells us about the effectiveness of Chinese espionage. That’s after the headlines. Five big stories UK | Ministers are considering changing the law to force the entertainment industry to better protect women and children in the wake of the revelations over David Walliams and the conviction of Russell Brand. Climate | The UK government has appointed the world’s first special representative for climate security, in the strongest sign yet of fears that climate breakdown will bring chaos to the country. US midterms | Democrat Scott Colom has become the first Black senator in Mississippi to be elected since Reconstruction, in a stunning upset after more than a week of vote counting in one of the country’s most reliably red states.

/news/2026/nov/12/russell-brand-accused-.headline: Farage was guest on Brand podcast after sexual assault investigation began
/news/2026/nov/12/russell-brand-accused-.excerpt: Nigel Farage appeared on Russell Brand’s US podcast nine months after police opened an investigation into the comedian after allegations of sexual assault, the Guardian has learned. The Reform UK leader has criticised Labour for “cosying up to” and “promoting” Brand a decade ago, after the comedian was sentenced this week to more than 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault. It has now emerged that Farage was a guest on Brand’s online show in July 2024 – months after allegations of sexual assault against Brand were first made public in media reports, but before he was charged in April 2025. During the episode, Farage laughed with Brand about their shared interests in taking on the establishment and suggested the west had provoked Vladimir Putin into the Ukraine war because “what you don’t do with a Russian bear is deliberately poke it with a stick”. Farage was aware of the serious sexual assault allegations against Brand at the time because he had commented on them on GB News the previous year, but they were not mentioned in the episode. Sitting on a sofa with Brand alongside Dan Bongino, a Donald Trump supporter, and Charlie Kirk, the rightwing activist later murdered, Farage spoke of how “the old left-right divides” were being blown out of the water. He claimed that cancel culture meant people saying racist or homophobic things were “cancelled” but contempt for the white working class was allowed.

/news/2026/nov/12/russell-brand-accused-.headline: Judge who sentenced Russell Brand praised for dispelling rape myths
/news/2026/nov/12/russell-brand-accused-.excerpt: The judge who sentenced Russell Brand has been praised for dispelling rape myths with “piercing clarity”. Mr Justice Bennathan’s sentencing remarks were particularly welcomed given that rape myths had played a part in the trial. He was also lauded for calling out “enablers” who witnessed sexual assaults by the comedian. Sentencing Brand to 10 and a half years on Monday for raping a woman and sexually assaulting three others, Bennathan said: “Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent.” Andrew Thomas KC, the chair of the Criminal Bar Association, and Kama Melly KC, its vice-chair, said: “We welcome the piercing clarity of the judge’s statement. Myths about rape and sexual assault must play no part in our culture or in our courtrooms. Raping or sexually assaulting someone is a crime, and blame lies entirely with the perpetrator. “Victims of sexual violence should know that when they go to the prosecution authorities, their evidence will be judged fairly and properly. As the verdicts in Russell Brand’s case show, a properly directed jury will not be put off by a defendant’s appeal to rape myths.” Ciara Bergman, the chief executive of Rape Crisis England & Wales, said Bennathan’s remarks were “hugely important” at the end of such a high-profile trial.

Shortly after Brand was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison, Goldsmith posted on X: “I am in awe of the courageous women who came forward at Brand’s trial, told their stories, testified and ensured justice was done. “I have had my own personal experience of his violence, coercive control and abuse. I had to call the police to have him removed from my house in 2014 during a violent incident. Whilst my pain in relation to this pales in comparison to what the women have testified in court have suffered, this was a difficult period in my life which has had a lasting impact.” On Thursday, Brand was found guilty of raping a fan and sexually assaulting three women in separate incidents between 2004 and 2009. He was cleared of two further charges of rape and one of attempted indecent assault.

/news/2026/nov/12/russell-brand-accused-.headline: Russell Brand sentenced to more than 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault
/news/2026/nov/12/russell-brand-accused-.excerpt: Russell Brand was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison on Monday after a judge praised his victims’ bravery and accused him of living “unhindered by the rules by which decent people live”. As the judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, sentenced Brand for raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others, he said he had told the trial “a series of lies”. The disgraced comedian had displayed a “casual, arrogant disregard of any woman’s right to say no”, he said. “About 20 years ago, Russell Brand, you were becoming famous. You were clever – and in many people’s eyes, funny and charismatic. You had also become a sexual predator,” the judge said. “Whatever women wear, wherever they go, whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and demand justice in the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Mr Brand, act without their consent.” Brand’s sentencing, the culmination of a four-week trial at Southwark crown court, came after the four women described the impact of his crimes on their lives in victim impact statements. A woman who was raped by Brand said the attack had had lasting consequences. “Even now, I feel that I am living with the trauma of what happened,” she said. “It is something I carry with me every day and it often feels never-ending.” Brand, 51, appeared emotionless as he was jailed, but told his wife, Laura: “We’ll be OK,” as he was taken downstairs by the dock officers. His wife replied: “I love you,” before leaving the court in tears.

She read out her own statement, saying: When it happened I was in complete shock and turmoil for weeks trying to process what had happened to me, I was extremely upset and traumatised. I literally lost any love for myself for a long time, thinking that I was damaged goods. I felt vulnerable whenever I was going for an evening out for a long time after it happened, scared of giving off any signals that could be taken the wrong way. That undeserved feeling of shame and ‘what if I’d done this or done that’ has been carried around inside me for over 20 years, always there even when I’ve tried to compartmentalise and get on with my life. Seven people were arrested in Birmingham on Saturday after fireworks were set off in the city centre on Halloween, while the landlady of a Salford pub told how it was surrounded by “about 60 teenagers”, who shot fireworks at the building and harassed passersby. /world/2026/nov/13/ukraine-war-briefing-.excerpt: Russia and Ukraine have agreed to the “largest prisoner exchange” of the war at their first US-brokered talks since February but made little progress towards a broader peace agreement. Both sides sent senior delegations to the two-day talks, led by Donald Trump’s envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, in an effort to find a solution to end the nearly-five-year war. David Arakhamia, a senior member of Ukraine’s delegation, said the Russian team had arrived with “very, very strict directives”, making it difficult to narrow differences. But he said there had been “really big progress” on security guarantees for Ukraine after the war. “I think we have good momentum to bring about a solution before the new year,” Arakhamia said. Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, also struck an upbeat tone, saying he could see a path to an agreement. “These deals are very hard and complex, and this one is very emotional, very complex. It’s a very hot war,” he said. “But we see all the different ingredients to make a deal. We just have to figure out how to refine those ingredients, organise them and create the right structure and pathway.” Kushner said the planned exchange, expected to involve more than 1,000 prisoners from each side, would “reunite families, build trust and create momentum towards peace”.

/world/2026/nov/13/ukraine-war-briefing-.headline: Ukraine captures first Indonesian prisoner of war amid surge in Russian recruitment
/world/2026/nov/13/ukraine-war-briefing-.excerpt: Ukraine says it has captured its first Indonesian prisoner of war, amid what it says is a spike in recruitment by Russia from the south-east Asian nation. The 49-year-old man from Java was taken to Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region to take part in a Russian assault, but managed to reach Ukrainian-held territory after the group came under drone attack, according to Ukraine’s state-run I Want to Live project. He was then captured by the Ukrainians. According to the project, some 283 Indonesians were recruited in the first nine months of this year to fight for Russia against Ukraine. It said recruitment from Indonesia was no more than 10 in the previous three years. The Russian embassy in Jakarta did not immediately respond to questions about the alleged recruitment effort but it is not the first time Russia has sought foreign mercenaries for its war effort. In February, Kenya’s intelligence services reported that more than 1,000 Kenyans had been lured to fight for Russia. A growing number of people from African countries – including Kenya, Uganda and South Africa – and elsewhere have been lured to the frontline as Russia seeks help to sustain its more than four-year war after invading Ukraine in February 2022. This month Jakarta urged Moscow to ensure no Indonesians were drafted into its military, following the reported death in October of an Indonesian national serving with the military.

Mohammadi said on his Telegram channel that the Americans had proposed a timeframe of about two weeks after which Donald Trump would make a decision on military action. Mohammadi, who is regarded as a reliable indicator of Ghalibaf’s thinking, cast doubt on the US president’s claim that the military option was off the table. Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani, the emir of Qatar, spoke to Donald Trump about the proposal, the emir’s office said on Friday without revealing the call’s contents. The state news agency said the emir “emphasised the importance of continuing dialogue and embracing diplomacy as a means of resolving disputes, preventing further escalation in the region”. Trump is still considering whether to mount a further assault on Iranian nuclear sites, though the credibility of his threats is weaker inside Iran after his vice-president, JD Vance, said the war itself, and not just its cost to American consumers, was critical to the collapse of the Republican vote in the US midterms. Under the Qatar proposal, the US would immediately lift the naval blockade on Iran in the strait of Hormuz and release a portion of the $8bn (£6bn) of its frozen assets. In return, Iran would agree to visits by International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors to its bombed nuclear facilities, based on a previous abandoned agreement that had been reached in Cairo in September 2025.

/us-news/2026/nov/12/trump-jd-vance-iran.headline: Russia agreed to supply Iran with 90 helicopter missile launchers
/us-news/2026/nov/12/trump-jd-vance-iran.excerpt: Russia arranged to supply Iran with 90 launchers for advanced guided missiles, according to leaked defence industry documents that shed light on the depth of military cooperation between Moscow and Tehran. The documents, obtained by Dallas Analytics, a Ukrainian private intelligence firm, and shared with the Guardian, detail plans to supply Iran with launchers for the LMUR, a guided missile fired from attack helicopters which Russian forces have used extensively against Ukrainian targets since the full-scale invasion in 2022. A production schedule drawn up in May 2024 by Vympel, a leading Russian designer of missiles and launch systems, lists an order for 90 launchers under an export contract designated “K-10”, with deliveries scheduled between late 2024 and December 2025. Separate internal paperwork explicitly identifies K-10 as Iran. The records do not establish whether the launchers were ultimately delivered. However, a separate production schedule listing six Yak-130 jet trainers destined for Iran in 2023 is consistent with publicly reported deliveries of the aircraft. The files offer fresh insight into Russian-Iranian military cooperation at a sensitive moment as Washington weighs its next steps in its war against Iran after the US midterm elections. Observers widely regard Moscow as one of the main winners of a prolonged war in Iran, which has brought Russia strategic and economic advantages.
